subtopic_detail: Choosing between alkalinisation and dialysis in adolescent salicylate poisoning with a falling pH
stem:
You are the registrar in a tertiary emergency department. A 15-year-old girl is brought in 6 hours after taking an unknown quantity of her grandmother's aspirin tablets following an argument. She has vomited three times and says her ears are ringing.

She weighs 52 kg. She takes no regular medicines and has no medical history. She is agitated but oriented and answers questions appropriately.

She has already received 2 L of intravenous sodium bicarbonate infusion with potassium supplementation over the past 2 hours, and her urine pH is 7.6. Her serum salicylate concentration was 640 mg/L at 4 hours and is 810 mg/L on the repeat sample taken 2 hours later. Arterial blood gas on presentation showed pH 7.47, pCO2 22 mmHg, bicarbonate 16 mmol/L. The repeat gas now shows pH 7.29, pCO2 21 mmHg, bicarbonate 10 mmol/L. Creatinine is 74 micromol/L (45-90) and she is passing urine freely.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 128/min, blood pressure 104/62 mmHg, respiratory rate 34/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 38.4 °C
data_table.Investigations: Salicylate 640 mg/L at 4 hours rising to 810 mg/L at 6 hours; initial gas pH 7.47, pCO2 22 mmHg, bicarbonate 16 mmol/L; repeat gas pH 7.29, pCO2 21 mmHg, bicarbonate 10 mmol/L; creatinine 74 micromol/L (45-90)
data_table.Treatment so far: 2 L intravenous sodium bicarbonate with potassium over 2 hours; urine pH 7.6

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange urgent haemodialysis while continuing the bicarbonate infusion and correcting potassium
options.rationale: A rising concentration above 700 mg/L together with a falling arterial pH despite adequate urinary alkalinisation meets the criteria for extracorporeal removal, and each feature independently would justify it. The fall in pH is the critical change, because acidaemia shifts salicylate into the non-ionised form that crosses into the brain. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology)

options.text: Continue the bicarbonate infusion alone and repeat the salicylate concentration in 2 hours
options.rationale: Alkalinisation has already been delivered to a urine pH of 7.6 and the concentration is still climbing while the arterial pH falls, so persisting without escalation allows deterioration. Continued alkalinisation alone would be correct if the concentration were falling and the arterial pH were stable or rising. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology)

options.text: Give repeated doses of activated charcoal every 4 hours and repeat the concentration in 2 hours
options.rationale: Multiple dose charcoal can limit ongoing absorption from a concretion but does not remove salicylate already distributed to tissue, and it carries aspiration risk in a vomiting, agitated patient. It would be a useful adjunct earlier in a protected, non-vomiting patient with a rising concentration. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology)

options.text: Perform rapid sequence intubation with controlled ventilation and repeat the concentration in 2 hours
options.rationale: Intubation in salicylate poisoning is hazardous because any drop in minute ventilation during the apnoeic period worsens acidaemia and can precipitate cardiac arrest. It would be necessary only for airway failure or exhaustion, and then with ventilation matched to the pre-intubation respiratory rate. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology)

options.text: Give intravenous acetylcysteine by the standard infusion regimen and repeat the concentration in 2 hours
options.rationale: Acetylcysteine treats paracetamol toxicity by replenishing glutathione and has no role against salicylate, which causes oxidative phosphorylation uncoupling rather than a reactive metabolite injury. It would be indicated if a co-ingested paracetamol concentration sat above the treatment line. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology)

explanation.summary: Salicylate poisoning produces a characteristic mixed picture of respiratory alkalosis from direct respiratory centre stimulation superimposed on a high anion gap metabolic acidosis from uncoupled oxidative phosphorylation. The initial gas here shows the alkalotic phase, and the transition to acidaemia marks the point at which the patient is decompensating rather than improving. That transition is dangerous out of proportion to the numbers, because salicylate is a weak acid whose non-ionised fraction rises as pH falls, allowing it to cross the blood-brain barrier and cause cerebral oedema, seizures and death. Urinary alkalinisation works by trapping ionised salicylate in the tubule and is the mainstay of moderate poisoning, but once it has been optimised and concentrations still rise, only extracorporeal removal will clear the drug. Salicylate concentrations should be repeated every 2 hours until falling, because delayed and erratic absorption from tablet concretions means a single value never excludes serious toxicity.
key_points: Expect mixed respiratory alkalosis with high anion gap metabolic acidosis; a falling pH signals decompensation
Acidaemia increases the non-ionised fraction that crosses into the brain, so pH matters more than concentration alone
Haemodialysis is indicated for concentrations above roughly 700 mg/L, acidaemia, altered mental state, or renal failure
Intubation is high risk because loss of compensatory hyperventilation can precipitate arrest
Repeat concentrations every 2 hours until clearly falling, because absorption is delayed and erratic
explanation.pearls: If intubation becomes unavoidable in salicylate poisoning, match the ventilator to the patient's own pre-intubation minute ventilation, often above 30 breaths per minute, rather than to conventional lung-protective settings.

subtopic_detail: Chelation threshold and source control for an asymptomatic child with an elevated blood lead level
stem:
You are the registrar in a general paediatric clinic in a mining town. A 3-year-old boy is referred after a community screening program found an elevated blood lead level. His parents report no symptoms and say he is a fussy eater who frequently puts dirt and paint flakes in his mouth.

The family lives in a weatherboard house built in 1950 with peeling exterior paint. His father works at the smelter and changes out of his work clothes at home.

On examination he is alert and playful with a normal neurological examination, no abdominal tenderness and no gum line. Development is age-appropriate. Venous blood lead is 28 micrograms/dL on a confirmatory sample, repeated from an initial capillary result of 31 micrograms/dL. Haemoglobin is 104 g/L (110-140) with a mean cell volume of 68 fL (75-87) and ferritin 9 micrograms/L (15-150). Abdominal radiograph shows no radio-opaque foreign material.

data_table.Examination: Alert and playful, neurological examination normal, abdomen non-tender, no gum line, development age-appropriate
data_table.Investigations: Venous blood lead 28 micrograms/dL (confirmatory, after capillary 31 micrograms/dL); haemoglobin 104 g/L (110-140), mean cell volume 68 fL (75-87), ferritin 9 micrograms/L (15-150); abdominal radiograph shows no radio-opaque material
data_table.Exposure: 1950 weatherboard house with peeling exterior paint; father works at the smelter and changes clothing at home; frequent mouthing of dirt and paint flakes

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Admit for intravenous sodium calcium edetate chelation, treat the iron deficiency and repeat the lead level
options.rationale: Parenteral chelation is reserved for encephalopathy or levels at or above 70 micrograms/dL, and this child is asymptomatic at 28 micrograms/dL. It would be correct for a child with seizures, altered consciousness or a level in that range. (Source: NHMRC: Managing individual exposure to lead in Australia)
source_refs: NHMRC: Managing individual exposure to lead in Australia

options.text: Notify public health for source assessment, treat the iron deficiency and repeat the lead level
options.rationale: Below the chelation threshold the interventions that lower a blood lead level are removal of the source and correction of iron deficiency, because iron deficiency upregulates the divalent metal transporter that absorbs lead from the gut. A level of 5 micrograms/dL or above is notifiable in Australian jurisdictions and triggers the environmental investigation that addresses both the paint and the take-home occupational exposure. (Source: NHMRC: Managing individual exposure to lead in Australia)
source_refs: NHMRC: Managing individual exposure to lead in Australia

options.text: Commence oral succimer chelation as an outpatient, treat the iron deficiency and repeat the lead level
options.rationale: Oral chelation is generally considered from about 45 micrograms/dL, and trials at lower levels showed no cognitive benefit while the level rebounded once the drug stopped. Succimer would be appropriate for a symptomatic child or one in that higher band with the source already removed. (Source: NHMRC: Managing individual exposure to lead in Australia)
source_refs: NHMRC: Managing individual exposure to lead in Australia

options.text: Give a calcium and vitamin D supplement, treat the iron deficiency and repeat the lead level
options.rationale: Adequate dietary calcium modestly reduces lead absorption and is part of general advice, but supplementation alone does not lower an established level while exposure continues. It would be a reasonable adjunct once the environmental source had been identified and controlled. (Source: NHMRC: Managing individual exposure to lead in Australia)
source_refs: NHMRC: Managing individual exposure to lead in Australia

options.text: Arrange whole bowel irrigation with polyethylene glycol, treat the iron deficiency and repeat the lead level
options.rationale: Bowel irrigation is used to clear ingested radio-opaque lead objects or paint chips seen on imaging, and this radiograph shows none. It would be correct where a retained lead foreign body such as a swallowed sinker or fragment were visible. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology)

explanation.summary: Childhood lead exposure in Australia clusters around older housing with deteriorating pre-1970 paint, mining and smelting communities, and take-home contamination on parental work clothing, all three of which are present in this family. There is no threshold below which lead is known to be safe, and the cognitive effects are subclinical at the levels most children present with, so the absence of symptoms is expected rather than reassuring. The counterintuitive part of management is that chelation is not the answer for most elevated levels: it lowers the measured blood concentration without demonstrated cognitive benefit at moderate levels, and the level rebounds from bone stores once treatment stops. Source removal is the only intervention that changes long-term body burden, which is why notification and an environmental health assessment do more than any drug. Iron deficiency deserves specific attention because it both increases gastrointestinal lead absorption and independently harms development, so the two problems compound each other.
key_points: Blood lead of 5 micrograms/dL or above is notifiable in Australia and triggers environmental investigation
Source removal and correction of iron deficiency are the interventions that lower body burden at moderate levels
Oral chelation is generally considered from about 45 micrograms/dL; parenteral therapy for encephalopathy or 70 micrograms/dL and above
Chelation at moderate levels lowers the blood concentration without demonstrated cognitive benefit and is followed by rebound from bone
Take-home exposure on parental work clothing is a recognised route in smelting and mining communities
explanation.pearls: Iron deficiency increases lead absorption through the shared divalent metal transporter 1 in the duodenum, so replacing iron in a lead-exposed child lowers the level independently of any chelating agent.

sources.label: NHMRC: Managing individual exposure to lead in Australia

subtopic_detail: Whether to continue antibiotic prophylaxis after a second febrile urinary infection with high grade reflux
stem:
You are the registrar in a paediatric nephrology clinic. A 14-month-old girl is reviewed after her second febrile urinary tract infection, both grown Escherichia coli, treated 5 weeks ago and 4 months ago.

She was born at term with no antenatal renal abnormality detected on the 20 week morphology scan. Her mother reports normal wet nappies and no constipation. She is not yet toilet trained.

She is thriving on the 60th centile. Blood pressure is 92/54 mmHg. Renal ultrasound performed after the second infection shows bilateral hydronephrosis with dilated ureters and normal cortical thickness. A micturating cystourethrogram performed after the second infection shows grade IV vesicoureteric reflux on the left and grade III on the right, with no posterior urethral valve. Creatinine is 26 micromol/L (15-35). Her latest urine culture after treatment is sterile and she is currently taking no medication.

data_table.Vital signs: Blood pressure 92/54 mmHg, remaining vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Investigations: Renal ultrasound: bilateral hydronephrosis with dilated ureters, normal cortical thickness. Micturating cystourethrogram: grade IV reflux left, grade III right, no posterior urethral valve. Creatinine 26 micromol/L (15-35). Post-treatment urine culture sterile
data_table.History: Two febrile Escherichia coli urinary tract infections 4 months and 5 weeks ago; no antenatal renal abnormality; no constipation

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Give no prophylaxis, advise prompt treatment of future infections, with nephrology follow-up and surveillance
options.rationale: Watchful waiting is supported for low grade reflux and for a single infection, but this child has had two febrile infections with grade IV reflux, where recurrence risk and renal scarring risk are both substantially higher. No prophylaxis would be appropriate for grade I or II reflux after a single infection. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection)

options.text: Refer for ureteric reimplantation surgery now, with paediatric nephrology follow-up and imaging surveillance
options.rationale: Surgery is reserved for breakthrough febrile infection on prophylaxis, progressive scarring, or reflux persisting beyond early childhood, because most reflux resolves as the intravesical ureteric tunnel lengthens with growth. Reimplantation would be correct after failure of medical management. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection)

options.text: Start daily low dose trimethoprim prophylaxis with paediatric nephrology follow-up and imaging surveillance
options.rationale: Recurrent febrile infection combined with high grade dilating reflux is the subgroup in which prophylaxis reduces recurrence, even though trials show no benefit for low grade reflux or a single infection. Trimethoprim is the standard Australian agent at a quarter of the treatment dose, given nightly while the reflux is expected to resolve spontaneously. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection)

options.text: Start daily low dose amoxicillin prophylaxis with paediatric nephrology follow-up and imaging surveillance
options.rationale: Amoxicillin achieves poor urinary concentrations relative to resistance rates in Escherichia coli and rapidly selects resistant organisms, so it is not used for urinary prophylaxis beyond the neonatal period. It is the preferred prophylactic agent only in infants under about 6 weeks, where trimethoprim is avoided. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Arrange a dimercaptosuccinic acid scan before any decision, with nephrology follow-up and imaging surveillance
options.rationale: A cortical scan documents established scarring but does not alter the decision to start prophylaxis in a child who already has proven high grade reflux and recurrent febrile infection. It would be useful later to establish a baseline of renal parenchymal damage for long-term follow-up. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection)

explanation.summary: Vesicoureteric reflux was historically treated aggressively on the assumption that reflux caused scarring and that preventing infection would prevent renal failure, but randomised trials substantially narrowed the indications for both prophylaxis and surgery. The current position is that prophylaxis provides a modest absolute reduction in recurrence concentrated in children with dilating grades III to V reflux and recurrent febrile infection, while conferring little benefit at lower grades and selecting for resistant organisms in everyone. This child sits squarely in the group where the evidence still supports treatment. Australian practice reserves the micturating cystourethrogram for atypical or recurrent infection rather than performing it routinely, and its findings here directly determine management. Most reflux resolves spontaneously as the child grows and the intravesical ureteric tunnel lengthens, so prophylaxis is a holding measure rather than a permanent commitment, and bladder and bowel dysfunction should be addressed once the child is toilet trained.
key_points: Prophylaxis benefit concentrates in dilating grade III to V reflux with recurrent febrile infection
Trimethoprim at a quarter of the treatment dose nightly is the standard Australian prophylactic agent
Amoxicillin is unsuitable for prophylaxis beyond the neonatal period because of resistance selection
Surgery follows breakthrough febrile infection on prophylaxis or progressive scarring, not initial diagnosis
Most reflux resolves spontaneously with growth, so prophylaxis is an interim measure
explanation.pearls: Breakthrough febrile urinary infection while adherent to nightly trimethoprim is the specific trigger that converts medical management into a surgical referral, so document adherence before attributing a recurrence to prophylaxis failure.

subtopic_detail: Surveillance plan after velamentous cord insertion is reported at the morphology scan
stem:
You are the resident in a hospital antenatal clinic. A 29-year-old woman attends at 20 weeks in her first pregnancy to discuss her morphology scan.

The pregnancy was conceived spontaneously and has been uncomplicated. She takes pregnancy multivitamins and has no medical history. She has no bleeding, no pain and reports normal foetal movements for gestation.

The scan report describes a single foetus with growth on the 45th centile and normal anatomy. The placenta is posterior and its lower edge is 55 mm from the internal os. The umbilical cord is reported to insert into the membranes 40 mm from the placental edge, with vessels running through the membranes toward the placental disc. Colour Doppler over the internal os shows no vessels crossing it. Her blood pressure is 108/66 mmHg and urinalysis is negative.

data_table.Vital signs: Blood pressure 108/66 mmHg, remaining vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Investigations: Morphology scan at 20 weeks: single foetus, growth 45th centile, normal anatomy, posterior placenta with lower edge 55 mm from internal os, cord inserting into membranes 40 mm from placental edge, no vessels crossing the internal os on colour Doppler. Urinalysis negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate plan?

options.text: Arrange planned caesarean section at 35 weeks after antenatal corticosteroids, with inpatient admission from 32 weeks
options.rationale: Early planned birth with admission is the pathway for confirmed vasa praevia, where unprotected vessels cross the internal os and can rupture at membrane rupture. It would be correct if colour Doppler had shown vessels over the os, which it specifically did not. (Source: RANZCOG: Vasa praevia)

options.text: Arrange repeat placental localisation at 32 weeks with continued routine antenatal care and no growth scans
options.rationale: Repeat localisation is the follow-up for a low-lying placenta, and this placenta sits 55 mm from the internal os, which is already well clear. Repeat localisation would be indicated if the lower edge were within 20 mm of the os. (Source: RANZCOG: Placenta praevia and placenta accreta spectrum)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Placenta praevia and placenta accreta spectrum

options.text: Arrange amniocentesis for foetal karyotype and microarray, with continued routine antenatal care thereafter
options.rationale: An abnormal cord insertion in isolation with normal anatomy and normal growth is not an indication for invasive testing. Amniocentesis would be considered if structural anomalies or soft markers were also present on the morphology scan. (Source: RANZCOG: Prenatal screening and diagnostic testing for fetal conditions)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Prenatal screening and diagnostic testing for fetal conditions

options.text: Arrange serial growth ultrasound scans from the early third trimester with continued routine antenatal care
options.rationale: Velamentous cord insertion without vessels over the internal os is associated with foetal growth restriction rather than with vasa praevia, so serial growth surveillance is the intervention that changes management. Routine care otherwise continues because the mode and timing of birth are not altered by the insertion site alone. (Source: RANZCOG: Vasa praevia)

options.text: Arrange low dose aspirin from today with continued routine antenatal care and no additional growth scans
options.rationale: Aspirin is given for pre-eclampsia risk reduction and must be started before 16 weeks to be effective, so commencing at 20 weeks offers little benefit. It would be correct if started at the first visit in a woman with recognised pre-eclampsia risk factors, which are absent here. (Source: RANZCOG: Hypertension in pregnancy)

explanation.summary: Velamentous cord insertion describes the cord inserting into the membranes rather than the placental disc, so the vessels run unprotected by Wharton jelly for some distance before reaching the placenta. Its clinical significance splits into two quite separate problems that are frequently conflated. If those unprotected vessels happen to run across the internal cervical os the condition is vasa praevia, which is catastrophic if membranes rupture unrecognised and therefore demands planned preterm caesarean birth. If they do not cross the os, as here, the relevant association is with impaired placental transfer and foetal growth restriction, and the appropriate response is growth surveillance. Velamentous insertion is considerably more common in twin pregnancies and after assisted reproduction, and deliberately examining the os with colour Doppler whenever it is reported is what separates the two pathways.
key_points: Velamentous insertion means the cord inserts into membranes, leaving vessels without Wharton jelly
Colour Doppler over the internal os distinguishes vasa praevia from an isolated abnormal insertion
Isolated velamentous insertion is associated with foetal growth restriction and warrants serial growth scans
Vasa praevia requires antenatal corticosteroids and planned caesarean birth before labour
Incidence is higher in multiple pregnancy and after assisted reproductive technology
explanation.pearls: Vasa praevia is defined by foetal vessels running within 20 mm of the internal os, so ask explicitly for that measurement whenever a velamentous or marginal cord insertion is reported rather than accepting the insertion description alone.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Placenta praevia and placenta accreta spectrum
RANZCOG: Prenatal screening and diagnostic testing for fetal conditions

subtopic_detail: Management of nocturnal hand paraesthesia developing in the third trimester
stem:
You are the resident in a hospital antenatal clinic. A 31-year-old woman at 32 weeks in her second pregnancy describes 3 weeks of tingling and numbness in both hands that wakes her at night and is relieved by shaking them over the side of the bed.

She works as a hairdresser and says her grip has felt clumsy when holding scissors. She has gained 14 kg this pregnancy and has noticed swollen fingers and ankles in the evenings. Her first pregnancy and birth were uncomplicated.

On examination there is sensory blunting over the palmar aspects of the thumb, index and middle fingers of both hands. Tapping over the flexor retinaculum reproduces the tingling bilaterally. Thenar bulk is preserved and abductor pollicis brevis power is 5/5. Reflexes are normal. Blood pressure is 112/70 mmHg, urinalysis shows no protein, and haemoglobin, thyroid function, liver function tests and platelets are all within normal limits.

data_table.Vital signs: Blood pressure 112/70 mmHg, remaining vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Bilateral sensory blunting over palmar thumb, index and middle fingers, percussion over the flexor retinaculum reproduces tingling, thenar bulk preserved, abductor pollicis brevis power 5/5, reflexes normal, mild peripheral oedema
data_table.Investigations: Urinalysis no protein; haemoglobin, thyroid function, liver function tests and platelets within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Refer for urgent surgical decompression of the flexor retinaculum and review the symptoms in 4 weeks
options.rationale: Surgery is reserved for persistent symptoms with motor involvement or failure of conservative measures after birth, and thenar bulk and power are preserved here. Decompression would be indicated for thenar wasting, weak thumb abduction or symptoms persisting well beyond the postpartum period. (Source: RANZCOG: Common musculoskeletal conditions in pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Common musculoskeletal conditions in pregnancy

options.text: Arrange a local corticosteroid injection into the carpal tunnel and review the symptoms in 4 weeks
options.rationale: Injection is a reasonable second-line option but is not the initial step when a simple non-invasive measure has not been tried in a self-limiting condition. It would be appropriate if splinting failed and symptoms remained disabling. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology)

options.text: Commence oral frusemide to reduce the peripheral oedema and review the symptoms in 4 weeks
options.rationale: Diuretics do not relieve this compression and reduce plasma volume in a pregnancy that depends on expansion for placental perfusion, so they are avoided for physiological oedema. Frusemide has a place in pulmonary oedema complicating severe pre-eclampsia, not in dependent swelling. (Source: RANZCOG: Hypertension in pregnancy)

options.text: Arrange nerve conduction studies of both upper limbs and review the symptoms in 4 weeks
options.rationale: Electrophysiology is unnecessary when the distribution and provoking features are typical and management would be conservative regardless of the result. It would be worthwhile if the distribution were atypical, symptoms were unilateral with wasting, or surgery were being planned. (Source: RANZCOG: Common musculoskeletal conditions in pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Common musculoskeletal conditions in pregnancy

options.text: Provide neutral position wrist splints for night-time use and review the symptoms in 4 weeks
options.rationale: Pregnancy-related median nerve compression without motor loss is managed conservatively because fluid shifts reverse after birth and most women resolve spontaneously within weeks to months. Neutral wrist splinting worn overnight addresses the nocturnal flexion posture that provokes symptoms and is the first-line intervention. (Source: RANZCOG: Common musculoskeletal conditions in pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Common musculoskeletal conditions in pregnancy

explanation.summary: Median nerve compression at the wrist affects a substantial minority of pregnancies and is driven by the same fluid retention that produces peripheral oedema, with the carpal tunnel being a rigid compartment that tolerates little extra volume. The symptoms are worst at night because sleep tends to be spent with the wrist flexed, which further narrows the tunnel, and the classic history is waking to shake the hand out. The important clinical distinction is between sensory symptoms alone, which are self-limiting and managed conservatively, and motor involvement with thenar wasting, which risks permanent deficit and warrants escalation. Most cases resolve within weeks to a few months of birth as the fluid shift reverses, so the counselling message is as important as the splint. Symptoms persisting past 6 months postpartum should prompt reassessment, since the pregnancy explanation no longer holds.
key_points: Nocturnal paraesthesia in the median distribution relieved by shaking the hand is the characteristic history
Fluid retention narrows a rigid compartment, so the condition parallels peripheral oedema
Preserved thenar bulk and thumb abduction power indicate sensory-only involvement suitable for conservative care
Neutral position night splints are first-line; corticosteroid injection is second-line
Diuretics are not used, and nerve conduction studies are reserved for atypical or motor presentations
explanation.pearls: Thenar wasting or weak thumb abduction converts this from a self-limiting nuisance into an indication for surgical referral during pregnancy, because axonal loss recovers poorly even after the oedema resolves.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Common musculoskeletal conditions in pregnancy
